new_leaves.label: Okunev Stelae
new_leaves.defn: The monumental stone stelae and sculpture of the Okunev culture of the Minusinsk Basin, South Siberia (c. 2500–1800 BCE): saber-shaped slabs of sandstone and granite up to four metres or more carved with masked anthropomorphic faces, solar signs and beasts, with petroglyphs and small carved amulets.
new_leaves.see: L1-2 Petroglyphs of the Mongolian Altai
new_leaves.axis: phases and sites, then holding institutions

new_leaves.label: Karasuk Bronzes
new_leaves.defn: Bronze knives, daggers and axes of the Karasuk culture of South Siberia and the Altai (c. 1500–800 BCE): curved single-edged knives with handles cast as animal heads, a realistic animal art that fed the later Scytho-Siberian Animal Style and reached Shang–Zhou China.
new_leaves.axis: phases and sites, then holding institutions

new_leaves.label: Pazyryk Felts and Carvings
new_leaves.defn: The art preserved in the frozen kurgans of the Pazyryk culture of the Altai (6th–3rd century BCE; Pazyryk, Bashadar, Tuekta, Ukok): appliqué and dyed felt hangings and saddle cloths with animal combat and investiture scenes, carved wooden griffins, elk and felines, leather cut-work, tattoos, and imported Persian and Chinese textiles including the Pazyryk carpet.
src: UNESCO Tentative List: Treasures of the Pazyryk Culture
new_leaves.axis: phases and sites, then holding institutions
kinds: earlier kurgans with carved wooden animals

new_leaves.label: Dilmun Seals
new_leaves.defn: Round stamp seals of steatite of the Dilmun civilization of Bahrain, Failaka and the eastern Arabian coast (c. 2050–1650 BCE), carved with gazelles, bulls, human figures and symbols, drawing on the Indus seal tradition; with the ridged Barbar pottery and the royal burial mounds.
src: UNESCO Memory of the World nomination
new_leaves.axis: phases and sites, then holding institutions

new_leaves.label: Jorwe Ware
new_leaves.defn: Black-on-red painted pottery of the Chalcolithic Jorwe culture of Maharashtra (c. 1400–700 BCE; Inamgaon, Daimabad, Walki): fine wheel-thrown spouted jars and carinated bowls painted with geometric patterns and occasionally deer and human figures.
new_leaves.axis: phases and sites, then holding institutions

new_leaves.label: Kura–Araxes Pottery
new_leaves.defn: The handmade red-black burnished ware of the Kura–Araxes (Early Transcaucasian) culture of the South Caucasus and eastern Anatolia (c. 3500–2450 BCE), with incised and relief spirals and geometric motifs, decorated hearth stands, spread to the Levant as Khirbet Kerak ware.
new_leaves.axis: phases and sites, then holding institutions

new_leaves.label: Beldibi Cave Art
new_leaves.defn: Coloured rock engravings and paintings of the Beldibi cave near Antalya (late Palaeolithic to proto-Neolithic, c. 10,000 BCE), the only known cave art in western Asia, with portable stones carved with naturalistic animals and geometric ornament.
new_leaves.axis: phases and sites, then holding institutions
kinds: neighbouring cave of the same sequence
